yt_title: Quoting Software for Manufacturing: A Job Shop Guide (AU & NZ)
yt_desc:
Read the full guide: https://zudoworks.com/insights/quoting-software-for-manufacturing/

A manufacturing quote is a promise about cost, made before the job exists. This short explainer walks through how a small fabrication or machining shop builds a quote that holds up a month later, and where quoting software helps.

Chapters
00:00 A quote is a promise about cost
00:04 The four parts of every quote
00:08 Material from the bill of materials
00:13 Labour: hours times a shop rate
00:18 The trap: margin and markup
00:22 Worked example (Example figures)
00:31 Setup and batch size
00:35 Quote where jobs and stock live
00:41 Read the full guide

Key points from the guide
- Every quote for a made part has four parts: material, labour, setup and outside work, and margin. Software does the arithmetic; you supply the rates.
- Material comes from the bill of materials: each component, quantity per unit, a scrap allowance, at today's cost.
- Labour is hours per operation multiplied by the shop rate. The shop rate adds direct labour, fixed overhead and variable overhead per productive hour, so it is always higher than the wage.
- Markup is profit as a percentage of cost. Margin is profit as a percentage of price. Example: on a cost of $141.99 a unit, a 35% markup gives $191.69, while a 35% margin needs $218.45. That is $26.76 a unit apart.
- Setup belongs to the batch. Example: $78 of setup is $6.50 a unit in a batch of 12 and $0.78 a unit in a batch of 100.
- There are three kinds of quoting software: a spreadsheet, a tool that reads drawings, and quoting inside the system that runs the shop. For most small job shops making repeat and similar parts, quoting where jobs and stock live means every quote can be compared with the job's real cost.

The guide also covers GST on quotes in Australia and New Zealand, a checklist for choosing quoting software, and how quotes work in ZMOS, including what its quote form does not do.

Which do you quote on, margin or markup? Tell us in the comments.

linkedin_profile:
Many quoting mistakes in small shops are not software problems. They are arithmetic problems that software makes faster.

The one that costs the most money is also the easiest to miss: margin and markup are different numbers.

Here is the worked example from our new guide. Example figures, one sheet-metal enclosure in a batch of 12:

Material from the BOM, scrap included: $44.49
Labour, 1.40 hours at a $65 shop rate: $91.00
Setup, $78.00 spread over 12 units: $6.50
Cost: $141.99 a unit

Price it at a 35% margin and you charge $218.45.
Type 35 into a markup box instead and you charge $191.69, which is a margin of about 26%.

$26.76 a unit. $321.12 on the batch. Nobody notices until the year-end numbers.

Three habits that fix most of it:

1. Know what your software's percentage field means. Write it on the quoting procedure.
2. Build a real shop rate: direct labour plus fixed and variable overhead per productive hour. The wage alone never recovers the building.
3. Quote setup for the batch you are actually making. The same $78 of setup is $0.78 a unit in a batch of 100 and $6.50 in a batch of 12.

The guide also compares the three kinds of quoting software, and it is honest that a shop quoting hundreds of new CAD parts a month needs a tool that reads drawings.

What does your quoting tool's percentage field mean: margin or markup? I would genuinely like to know how many people have checked.
